question: In its reply to a previous question (E-000587/2022)1 on open access to scientific publications, the Commission sets out the efforts it makes to provide open access to scientific and academic publications, stating that public funds can be allocated to cover the necessary costs. Recent data shows that the cost of publishing is going up and up. It is a source of business for the sector’s publishers.

In 2022, one in four scientific articles in Portugal published by the five largest scientific publishers paid publication fees. For scientists and researchers, metrics like ‘impact factor’ are what causes the problem. Evaluation systems used for science funding place too great an emphasis on impact factor, at the expense of other aspects. Researchers feel obliged to publish because funding hinges on publications.
Although access to those academic articles is then free, publication itself uses allocated public money. 1.
What does the Commission make of publishers’ making money from public funds and the work of researchers and revisers?
Is the Commission, alongside the scientific community, willing to promote other impact factors that also acknowledge research results?
answer: The Commission is aware of the increasing costs of publishing and the implications on equity in scholarly publishing and sustainability of public research funding. It supports immediate and unrestricted open access to scientific publications, which is mandatory in Horizon Europe (2).
The Commission funded a study on scientific publishing in Europe that shows a pervasive lack of transparency of publishers’ costs of publishing and accessing scientific content (3).

The Commission is increasing its support to empower research organisations to improve their own publishing services and is funding numerous projects to this end, such as Developing Institutional open Access publishing Models to Advance Scholarly communication (DIAMAS) (4) and Creating a Robust Accessible Federated Technology for Open Access (CRAFT-OA) (5).

The Commission also supports its own open access publishing platform, Open Research Europe (ORE ) (6) and is exploring with the Member States and research funding organisations the possibility of transforming ORE into a collectively funded notfor-profit large-scale open access research publishing service for the public good.

The Commission has facilitated the process of drafting the Agreement on Reforming Research Assessment (7) and the establishment of the coalition of signatories, Coalition for Advancing Research Assessment (CoARA) (8). The Agreement calls, among others, for abandoning inappropriate uses of journal- and publication-based metrics, in particular the Journal Impact Factor (JIF) (9).

The Commission is a signatory and member of CoARA. Horizon Europe application forms require applicants to provide in their proposals a short qualitative assessment of the impact of their listed work instead of the JIF.
